overview.text: The Statue of Liberty, formally “Liberty Enlightening the World,” is a colossal copper figure on Liberty Island at the entrance to New York Harbor. French sculptor Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi designed it, with Gustave Eiffel’s firm responsible for its supporting framework. Proposed as a gift celebrating U.S. independence and French-American friendship, the statue was built in France, shipped in sections, reassembled in New York, and dedicated October 28, 1886. Its torch symbolizes enlightenment; the tablet bears July 4, 1776, in Roman numerals, and broken chains at her feet signify emancipation. Combining classical imagery with innovative engineering, it became both a national emblem and a symbol associated with immigration to the United States.

key_facts.text: The statue’s sculptor-given title is “Liberty Enlightening the World”; it stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor.
Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi designed the statue, and Gustave Eiffel’s firm engineered its framework.
Built in France and shipped to New York in sections, the statue was officially dedicated on October 28, 1886.
The torch represents enlightenment; the tablet shows July 4, 1776, in Roman numerals; broken chains at her feet symbolize the abolition of slavery.
Conceived as a gift affirming U.S.–French friendship, the statue also became a symbol associated with immigration to the United States.
